Pele Yoetz 62:82: It is forbidden to greet one's teacher first or to return his greeting [with an equal informal greeting], but rather one should not greet him at all, to fulfill "let even young men see me and hide themselves" (Job 29:8), or say "peace be upon you, my teacher and master." And likewise it is forbidden to call one's teacher or one's father and mother by their own name (Rambam, Hilchot Talmud Torah 1:3; see Sanhedrin 100a).
Pele Yoetz 62:83: It is forbidden to raise one's voice while others are praying or studying, for it causes confusion of their mind and nullifies their intention. And whoever assists those performing a mitzvah is given reward as one who performs the mitzvah (ibid. 99b).
Pele Yoetz 62:84: It is forbidden to disgrace any person, as we learned (Avot 4:3): do not despise any person. And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Derech Eretz Rabbah, ch. 5): treat every person as suspect as a robber, to guard against them, yet honor him as [you would] Rabban Gamliel. And whoever calls his fellow a slave or a wicked man (see Kiddushin 28a), or reviles and blasphemes with other insults, is liable to excommunication or a fine - and even toward small children it is not good to revile and insult, and especially if one calls them "accursed," which involves excommunication, and if one calls them "donkeys" or some other name of unclean animals or beasts, it causes the husk called by that name to attach itself to his soul. And many are not careful about this and call a child "donkey" or "dog," and one must inform them that they thereby injure a soul. Therefore let them be careful and not let unclean names be heard from their mouths. And how very much must preachers be careful not to disgrace the public - and when they preach about some matter people are not careful of, even if it is written in a book that many of the common people do such-and-such, they should speak in clean language and say "and many of the multitude of the people" and the like - a person should always speak in clean language (Pesachim 3a; see Yalkut Shimoni, Noach, remez 55) - in a manner that there be no element of disgrace and no room for anyone to take offense.
Pele Yoetz 62:85: And a person should always speak in clean language and not let a disgraceful word come from his mouth - for Scripture went out of its way for eight letters rather than mention a disgraceful term, as it is written (Genesis 7:2), "and of the animal that is not [einenah] clean" [avoiding the term "unclean"]. And they have already said (Shir HaShirim Rabbah 1:7): a person's mouth reveals his wisdom about him - for "a fool speaks folly," while "one of understanding has knowledge, his lips speak clearly."
Pele Yoetz 62:86: And likewise one should not say something that can be understood in two ways, lest a listener suspect him of an intention he did not have. And he should not rely on the fact that a discerning person will understand after examination, for the Tanna warned (Avot 2:4): do not say something that cannot be understood at first hearing, thinking that eventually it will be understood. And many times a division and a blazing fire result from someone speaking an obscure matter and a listener suspecting that his intention is for evil - and by the time he explains his intention, the flame has already risen, and who knows whether his words will be believed or not. Therefore let him be careful that his own understanding of his lips be spoken clearly, so that there be no room to err about his words and suspect him of evil. And likewise one must be very careful not to open his mouth to Satan unintentionally - for example, if he says "I shall not do this thing again," let him say it in the manner people customarily say "in health and in life" (in the vernacular: "shalud y vida," and in German: "bei Gesundheit und Leben"). And one must stand guard very much over this, especially when speaking with his fellow, so that if a mishap occurs, God forbid, there be no room to attribute it to his words as an unintended consequence proceeding from the ruler [i.e., from his own careless remark]. And I heard from a certain sage that once a man went on a journey and another accompanied him partway, and after the traveler had parted from him and gone some distance, the one who had accompanied him remembered to tell him something and called him by name - and the traveler turned back, out of respect for the Torah scholar, to see what he would call him for - and the sage wanted to say "do not go back," but immediately remembered that it was not good to say such a thing to one going on a journey, and said to him instead, simply, "wait." And of all such matters, let the wise man hear and increase learning. And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, already warned (Mo'ed Katan 27b) of a similar case, not to say to a sick person or a mourner who wishes to rise out of respect for an elder and the like, "do not get up," but rather to say to him, "do not trouble yourself, sit calmly." And diligence leads to care.
Pele Yoetz 62:87: It is forbidden to read or write words of Torah without reciting the Torah blessing. And matters that are in writing are forbidden to be recited orally (Gittin 60b) if they are not customarily fluent in everyone's mouth - and even regarding Psalms, there is one who has doubts about reciting it by heart. And it is better, if one needs this, to recite Mishnayot and the like - the Oral Torah that is fluent in his own mouth, and the Written Torah that is fluent in everyone's mouth, even if he repeats it a hundred times. And likewise it is forbidden to mention a matter of holiness without washing the hands, if his hands are not clean.
Pele Yoetz 62:88: One should not reveal to the common people the reasons for prohibitions, even those that are rabbinic, so that they not come to treat them lightly - for they said (Orach Chaim 128:2) that when one answers Amen after "Boneh Yerushalayim" in Grace after Meals, he should answer quietly, so that people not know that the blessing "HaTov VeHaMeitiv" is rabbinic and come to treat it lightly. And likewise there are several matters that are forbidden to be said in the presence of the common people, such as certain Aggadot and the like.
Pele Yoetz 62:89: Matters that are permitted, but that people have treated as forbidden according to the view of some stringent authority - you are not permitted to permit them in their presence, as long as no sword and mishap result [from continuing to be strict].
Pele Yoetz 62:90: One does not respond regarding a mishap, and of one who brings bad news it is said (Proverbs 10:18), "he who spreads slander is a fool" - unless it is necessary, in which case he shall tell it by hint.
Pele Yoetz 62:91: "You shall not favor them" (Deuteronomy 7:2) - you shall not give them favor (Avodah Zarah 20a). It is forbidden to say, "how fine is this gentile!" or to praise their deeds, for whatever kindness they do, they do for their own sake.
Pele Yoetz 62:92: Whoever hands over a Jew's body or his money into the hands of an idolater has no share in the World to Come, and it is permitted to save the victim even at the cost of the informer's life, even in this age.
Pele Yoetz 62:93: Whoever says to his fellow, "you did me no favor, so I too shall do you none," transgresses "you shall not take vengeance" (Leviticus 19:18). And if he does him a favor but says, "I am not like you [who withheld it from me]," he transgresses "you shall not bear a grudge" (Yoma 23a).
Pele Yoetz 62:94: Whoever recounts his fellow's good fortune and praise and does not bless him that the evil eye not have power over him and that he continue to increase and spread, causes evil to his fellow, and the cup shall also pass to him - as he has done, so shall it be done to him. Rather, "he who is good of eye shall be blessed," and the one who blesses shall himself be blessed from on high with abundant blessings and seven-fold favors.
Pele Yoetz 62:95: Behold, I have now arranged most of the matters from the categories of mitzvah, permitted, and forbidden speech - and if you examine closely, you shall find still more and more. And the pure man, before he brings forth any speech from his mouth, shall take to heart to clarify that speech - if it belongs to the category of mitzvah or the permitted, without any hint of prohibition, let him speak; and if not, let the two walls the Holy One, blessed be He, made - namely the teeth and the lips - remain closed, and let him not breach the fence of the King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, for "whoever breaches a fence, a serpent shall bite him" (Proverbs 21:23), and "he who guards his mouth and his tongue guards his soul from troubles" (Ecclesiastes... actually Proverbs 21:23 combined).
Pele Yoetz 62:96: And the source of all impurity is idle conversation, of which, with much speech, transgression does not cease, and all its companions are brought along after it. And even if none of these prohibitions results from it, it is itself a transgression - for our holy Rabbis, of blessed memory, whom whoever calls himself by the name of Israel believes in and in their words, said (Yoma 19b) that one who speaks idle words - and it is written (Ecclesiastes 1:8), "all words are wearisome, a man cannot express it" - and they said in the Midrash (Shemot Rabbah 13:1) on the verse (Malachi 2:17), "you have wearied the LORD with your words": the Holy One, blessed be He, said, I created all the worlds and there was no weariness before Me, as it is written (Isaiah 40:28), "He does not faint nor grow weary" - with what am I wearied? With whoever speaks idle words before Me. Woe to the one born of woman who causes this to a high and exalted King. And we learned (Avot 3:10): sitting in the assemblies of the common people removes a person from the world. And according to the teaching of the pious ones, idle words include the prohibition of scoffing, for we learned (ibid. verse 2): two who sit together without words of Torah between them, this is a session of scoffers. And we learned in the chapter on the acquisition of Torah (ibid. 6:2): Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said, every single day a heavenly voice goes out from Mount Horeb and proclaims and says, woe to these creatures for the disgrace of the Torah - for whoever does not occupy himself with Torah constantly (so it is in Avot D'Rabbi Natan) is called rebuked. And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Yerushalmi Chagigah 1:7) that an hour of neglect of Torah is equated with idolatry, forbidden sexual relations, and bloodshed.
Pele Yoetz 62:97: Correspondingly, I say, alas, alas, woe to us on the day of judgment, that the enemy, the inclination, has so overpowered a person that he must speak and hear words of novelty, and what advantage does the master of the tongue have - what does it give him, what does it add to him? And come and see how much the enemy has prevailed, that when brothers sit together and have no novel matter to speak of, they resort to the cold of the day, the heat of the day, the good rain, the good snow, and similar things known to all - because their inclination rattles within them and it is a disgrace to them to sit in silence, so they must begin with words until the conversation draws on from one matter to another. And even one who has no inclination for such talk seeks something to say, so that people not say to him, "why are you silent" - and this is folly, for he could simply excuse himself and say, "I have nothing to say, and there is nothing new."
Pele Yoetz 62:98: Therefore the man who fears the LORD shall not have his portion among those who sit in the corners, nor shall he sit in the session of scoffers who gather together for idle words - rather, let him go to the wise and become wise, or sit alone in his house doing his own work, the work of Heaven. And if at some time he is forced to sit in their company for the sake of the ways of peace and the like, let him be like one mute, not opening his mouth - and although this too is bad, for they said (Ketubot 5b): a person should not let his ears hear idle words, for they are the first to be burned among the limbs - nevertheless, since he cannot avoid it, let him choose the lesser evil, and let his heart tremble within him, and let him swiftly find himself an escape to leave their company as best he can, peacefully and equitably, through pretexts.
Pele Yoetz 62:99: And how good and how pleasant it would be if he strove to turn their words into words of holiness - for example, if they speak of the laws of kings and their wars, let him say to them: if so much preparation and strategy is made for this small war, all the more so must we do for the great war of the evil inclination; and if they give their very lives for their king, who is but worms and maggots like themselves, unable to give reward to those who do his will after death, all the more so must we give our lives for our Father, our King, the King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He; and if the king labors so hard with all his army to attain imagined honor, all the more so must we labor to attain the true honor in the eternal world. And let him say to them: what do you think - are all these wars by decree of the angelic princes? They are the wonder of the One perfect in knowledge, who watches over the lower worlds and brings about causes and transmigrations.
Pele Yoetz 62:100: And when they speak of business matters, let him mention to them the merchandise of Torah and mitzvot, for its merchandise is good. And when they mention some hardship or trouble, let him say to them: see, my sons, what sin causes - for a person does not stub his finger below unless it is decreed upon him from above (Chullin 7b), and no punishment comes into the world except for the sake of Israel [i.e., because of them] (Yevamot 63a; Rashi, Exodus 7:3). And when they mention something beloved and cherished, let him mention to them love of the Omnipresent. And when they mention a matter of fear, let him mention to them fear of the Omnipresent. And in this and that manner, let him strive to draw their words toward good things and tell them stories from the words of the Kabbalists and the Talmud and Midrashim and laws and the like. And if he does so, he shall merit and bring merit to others, and his reward shall increase. And in any case, if he cannot mention these things to them for some reason, let him mention them to himself, for a discerning man can find, from every single utterance, an arousal for his own soul. And if he hears them speaking some evil and forbidden words, let him say to them: please, my brothers, do not do evil; know that there is a prohibition in this speech and its prohibition is severe. And whatever is in his power to do to keep them from the prohibition, let him do, and the LORD shall be his help.
Pele Yoetz 62:101: And to you, men, I call: brothers and friends, I am greatly distressed for you, that this sin shall be your undoing and evil shall be before your faces, God forbid. And even greater than this is my own distress over the distress of our Father in Heaven, for He waits to be gracious to us, while our sins withhold the good from Him, besides the greatness of our own corruption and blemish. Therefore set your hearts and give honor to your God, and consider the time when you are free - such as on Sabbaths and festivals and the long nights, especially the nights following the Sabbath and the like - let it be more precious to you than precious stones and pearls, and let your heart tremble at spending bundle after bundle of time on such talk - for just as a mitzvah is elevated when performed by the many, correspondingly a transgression is greater and adds more strength to the Other Side when it is performed by the many. Exchange, please, evil for good - gather in the house of a Torah scholar, or one who knows books, to hear teachings, and recite Kaddish over the study - and this exchange shall seem to you like one who has risen from a deep pit to a high tower, and you shall attain the paths of life and an exalted ascent.
Pele Yoetz 63:1: Sermons - It is good to preach to the people the statutes of God and His teachings. And it is better to preach from a book than to preach orally, for several reasons. First, that one who preaches orally is prone to come to pride and the abomination of arrogance, which is not so when preaching from a book. Second, that one who preaches orally, if he says good things, is more likely to be affected by the evil eye, which is not so from within a book. Third, that one who preaches orally may find room to be exacting in his words when mentioning the punishment for transgressions people are accustomed to, as though cursing them directly, which is not so for one who preaches from a book. Fourth, for what can one innovate in our generation, in laws and words of ethics, beyond what is in the books of the commentators - are we not, in truth, like a monkey before a man compared to them? Fifth, for they said (Berachot 6b): every person who has fear of Heaven, his words are heeded. And they said (see Sefer Shirat Yisrael by Rabbi Moshe Ibn Ezra, page 156): words that come from the heart enter the heart. Therefore it is better to preach the words of the earlier generations, whose treasure was the fear of the LORD, and who preached fittingly and fulfilled fittingly (Chagigah 14b), and whose words came from the depth of the heart - which is not so for us, orphans of orphans. Sixth, that instead of taking the trouble and spending time to arrange a sermon, it is better to acquire proficiency and knowledge in laws and the like that he does not yet know, for the day is short and the work is much. Seventh, that whoever preaches a sermon written in a book does a kindness to the author, that his lips move in the grave, and what benefit have the sages who wrote books if there is none to expound and none to seek them?
Pele Yoetz 63:2: But what shall we do, since in these generations the words of the sages who preach orally are beloved, and when it is announced that there shall be an oral sermon, all the people from every corner come to the synagogue to hear the sermon - but to hear a sermon preached from a book, almost no one cares. And this is a matter without reason - for if they announced that the great rabbi so-and-so has come to the city and preaches from the pulpit, all the residents of the city would gather to hear his sermon, yet because it is written in a book, they do not wish to hear it. And if there were people who know how to read and could say "Torah is cast into a corner - is it not written in a book? When I have leisure I shall study this chapter" - they have remained silent [i.e. no such attitude prevails] - but the trouble is that such is the custom of the common masses, who do not know how to read a book, and it brings disgrace if, at a time when the custom is to preach an oral sermon, one wishes to preach from a book, for they would say, "this one is not a sage, but merely literate." And in such a case, where it is impossible to say "and clean" [i.e., to escape blame entirely], the counsel counseled is that the rabbi gather his oral sermon from pleasant things found in the books, bring [material] from the ordinary sources for that sermon, take to heart the great virtue of the earlier sages, and recognize his own small worth and limited understanding - let him state a matter in the name of the one who said it, and not clothe himself in a cloak not his own; and even if he added a touch or a grain of his own, he should not attribute it to his own name, for great is the evil of one who clothes himself in a cloak not his own, and whoever states a matter in the name of the one who said it brings redemption to the world (Avot 6:6).
Pele Yoetz 64:1: Making the Lips of the Sleeping Speak - "making the lips of the sleeping speak" (Song of Songs 7:10) - our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained that every Torah scholar in whose name a word of Torah is spoken in this world, his lips move in the grave (Yevamot 96b). And he has pleasure and peace of mind like one drinking spiced wine, as they said in the Yerushalmi of Shekalim (2:5). Therefore it is fitting for everyone whom the LORD has graced with knowledge to write and print a book according to his means, to benefit the many - performing a kindness to thousands - and it shall come to him for his own benefit, that he eat the fruit of his deeds, that his lips move in the grave at some time, for generations upon generations. And this is a true kindness that a person can do for the righteous, for the holy ones in the land whose portion is in life - to study their words, and their merit shall be a shield and protection over them. And it is already written in the books that once there was a persecution, and our teacher, the master Rabbi Moshe Alshich, of blessed memory, revealed himself while awake and saved a certain person from the midst of the upheaval, because of a reason that he was constantly studying his book. And how much more so if he takes trouble to resolve difficulties in their words, which is very valued by them. And see the book "Maggid Meisharim" (Parashat Vayakhel, page 80), which revealed to our master "Beit Yosef," of blessed memory, that the Rambam would intercede for him in Heaven above because he took trouble to explain and resolve his words, and at the time of his [the Rambam's] commemoration he would come to greet him. And it has already been brought in the introduction to Sefer "Magenei Shlomo" that because he took trouble to resolve Rashi's words against the difficulties of the Tosafot, he merited that at the time of his passing Rashi came to accompany him. Behold, therefore, how good it is to study the words of the Tannaim and Amoraim and the early rabbis and resolve their words, for their merit bursts forth and ascends. And it is good to study from all the books, for they are all equally good. And this obligation falls even more upon the offspring of the author of a book, for generations upon generations, to study the books of their forebears and resolve their words - for it is fitting for children to have mercy on their parents and give them a taste of pleasant things, and they [the parents] shall have mercy on them and intercede favorably for them like a father's compassion for his children (and see the introduction to Sefer "Chesed LeAvraham" by our master Rabbi Avraham Azulai). And this mitzvah likewise falls upon the community of a Torah scholar's own congregation, to study his words and repeat his hymns and the like, and thereby his merit shall shield them and hover over them all day.
Pele Yoetz 65:1: Plague - Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Bava Kamma 60b): if there is plague in the city, gather in your feet [stay indoors], or flee from the city at the beginning of the plague. And how good is the custom of the cities of Edom, who practice great caution and extra distancing - but on the other hand, it is not good to dwell in the cities of Edom, also for this reason: that if it happens, God forbid, that the attribute of judgment strikes someone because of excessive caution, they put him to death before his time with an unnatural death and burn him in the city, and he does not even receive burial, may the Merciful One save us. And it is better in the cities of Ishmael, where they strive for his healing and give him honor at his death through people assigned for this purpose. And in any case, an obligation rests upon every person to guard his own soul very much with extra caution in whatever comes to his hand, for it is written (Proverbs 22:3): "a clever man sees evil and hides himself, but the simple pass on and are punished." And they explained in the Holy Zohar (part 1, page 89) that for this alone, that he transgressed by not hiding himself, he deserves to be punished, and he is liable for his own life. And the essential protection is that if he distributes to the needy, the money shall not be considered [a loss to him], and the wealthy shall distribute greatly to sustain the souls of the poor, and this shall be an atonement for their own souls, that evil not befall them and no plague come near their tents. And they shall also offer prayer for their trouble every single day, and perform all the special remedies brought in the books, an order of studies, and especially reciting the order of the incense-mixture with intention, until the LORD looks favorably and grants peace in a land of life and tranquility.
Pele Yoetz 66:1: Putting Off - It has already been stated that putting off is not good, as it is written (Proverbs 3:28): "do not say to your neighbor, go and come back, and tomorrow I shall give." And it is written (ibid. 13:12): "hope deferred makes the heart sick." And it is written (Psalms 15:2): "and speaks truth in his heart" - meaning that he must say with his mouth what is in his heart. However, just as it is permitted to alter [the truth] for the sake of the ways of peace (Rashi, Genesis 50:16; see Yevamot 65b), so is it permitted to make excuses [i.e., delay] for the sake of the ways of peace, and especially for the sake of peace in the home - since women's minds are light, and if he tells her that he does not wish to fulfill her desire, even if he tells her of his distress that he cannot afford to fulfill all her wishes, there is a bad wife, may the Merciful One save us, who does not accept this and makes strife and quarrel - in such a case it is good for the man to put her off with vain and misleading excuses from day to day and from month to month, as he can, with good words, until Heaven has mercy on him. But where there is no concern about enmity and quarrel, truth shall guide his way, and he shall immediately state at the outset the thought and eventual outcome of the matter.
Pele Yoetz 66:2: However, this applies to matters where he can know the outcome, which is in his own hand - such as when they ask him for something and he does not wish to give it or do that thing. But regarding matters given over to Heaven, such as matchmaking, since "from the LORD is a wife for a man" - if matchmakers come to arrange a match for him or for his son, he should not reject them entirely by saying "I do not wish to take her" - for many times we have seen with our own eyes someone who despises a woman and has no desire for her at all, yet since she is his true match, when the time for marriage arrives his heart is turned within him to love her and he takes her as his wife - and these are the wonders of the One perfect in knowledge, who mixes matches. Behold, therefore, a person cannot say "I shall not take this woman" or "I shall not go to this city" and the like, for he does not know what a day may bring and what has been decreed upon him from Heaven. Therefore, when the matchmaker comes, let him put him off with words and say: if it is from Heaven, it can be - but there is still time before the appointed hour, for I do not yet wish to be matched; if the woman wishes, let her wait, and if she wishes, let her be matched [elsewhere]. And of all such matters, let the wise man hear and increase learning.
Pele Yoetz 66:3: And if putting off is bad in worldly matters, all the more so in matters of Torah and the improvement of the city - for if a person has a love of victory and sees what is right, yet nevertheless seeks to maintain his own words and opinion through vain and misleading, empty excuses, this man's evil is great, for it brings forth the sword, fire and flame, hatred and enmity, the permitting of a prohibition, and much mockery and weariness of the flesh. Therefore let a person be God-fearing and acknowledge the truth and what is right at the very outset of whatever he says, and through this he shall flourish like the palm tree.
Pele Yoetz 67:1: Laws - This is the Torah of the man whom the LORD has graced with knowledge, to be literate - this shall be Torah for its own sake, namely when it is to keep, to do, and to fulfill. Therefore he should not fail to study practical rulings every single day, to know what he should do - for those who do not know the laws walk in darkness and become soiled with every kind of impurity, and "the crooked shall be made straight" becomes instead "going and lacking," and the unwitting error of study for one who could have learned becomes counted as willful. Behold, therefore, studying the Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim, together with all the later halachic authorities, is an obligation to occupy oneself with daily, like prayer and tefillin, and likewise other laws necessary for every person - and it is because of our sins that error abounds due to lack of knowledge, and this causes an impure soul to descend into a child, may the Merciful One save us. Whoever is a man who desires life shall study Orach Chaim, and whoever desires that evil not befall him shall study Yoreh De'ah, and whoever does not know [Hebrew] books shall seek out vernacular books - but not rely on them to be lenient in practice, for sometimes there is something in the later books that is forbidden, yet it helps at least to be stringent, for whoever is stringent shall be blessed - but regarding a matter of leniency, he should act only according to a sage who is expert in the chambers of Torah, for "he who walks with the wise shall become wise" (Proverbs 13:20).
Pele Yoetz 67:2: And this is the evil of man upon the earth, that the forbidden seems to him like a straight path, and he does not enter the house of inquiry to ask, and even regarding what he doubts he does not know how to ask, but rather does what is right in his own eyes, and the way of leniency is preferable to him. Woe to us on the day of judgment, that a person shall be destined to give an account for not having sought to know the law - for exposition is not the essential thing, but rather the deed (Avot 1:17). Therefore, whatever new thing he learns or hears in his studies shall be recorded in his memory or written down, to be a remembrance between his eyes, to know what he should do and not transgress - for this is the whole point of study and listening. And in a case of doubt in the law, he shall be stringent, for it is fitting to fear transgressing the law more and more than one fears a sword - and even in a matter where the law has been settled leniently, a soul-conscious person shall be stringent with himself (and more is written on this in its place, for such is my way, to return to a subject) - and through this he shall be saved from destruction, and a blessing of good shall come upon him.
Pele Yoetz 68:1: Printing - Great is the benefit of printing in the world, through which Torah is magnified and its wellsprings spread outward. And behold, since mostly the hand of the sages is too limited to print their books, and they wear out their feet from city to city to gather money to print, it is fitting for the wealthy of the people of the God of Abraham to open their hands to them generously, and thereby they shall eat their portion equally with the sage, for "in the shade of wisdom is the shade of money" (Ecclesiastes 7:12). And everything depends on what kind of book it is, and on how needed it is by the many, and on the benefit that follows from it for the service of God, blessed be He. And examine closely and you shall find that there is hardly any money that could be counted for as great a mitzvah as this - for every expense for a mitzvah applies only to its own time, beginning with the mitzvah and finishing it, but whoever gives for the need of printing, his righteousness stands forever for generations upon generations, and he brings merit to the many - the merit of the many depends on him, and his righteousness shall go before him and after him. Happy is he, how good is his portion - he has acquired a good name, he has acquired for himself words of Torah, he has acquired for himself the life of the World to Come, and also this world - great money indeed.
Pele Yoetz 69:1: Dwelling - How much care is needed regarding the matter of dwelling - for they said (Berachot 8a-ish; actually referring to a general teaching): a person should always dwell in the place of his teacher, and if he can dwell near a Torah scholar he shall also find it good, and at the very least let him choose to dwell near a righteous, simple, and upright man - for this is like one who sits beside a perfume vendor and absorbs the good scent, while he should not dwell near an evil man, which is like sitting beside a naphtha seller and absorbing the bad odor. And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, already said (Avot 1:7): distance yourself from a bad neighbor. And they said (Nega'im 12:6): woe to the wicked man and woe to his neighbor; good for the righteous man and good for his neighbor. Only, whoever is a neighbor of a Torah scholar should go to him constantly and learn from his ways - for if not, it is better that he not dwell near him at all, for he shall be doubly punished for having had the opportunity to learn and not learning. And also regarding cities, a person should choose in which city to dwell, as I have written elsewhere, and especially to dwell in the Land of Israel - for they said (Ketubot 110b) that whoever dwells in the Land of Israel is as one who has a God, and so on - and it is known that Jerusalem is holier than the rest of the Land of Israel. Therefore, whoever's soul longs and strives to dwell honorably in our land shall choose the good for himself: it is good to establish his dwelling in Jerusalem, the holy city, may it be built and established speedily in our days - unless he thinks that in another city he shall have more settledness for the service of God, blessed be He, in which case even dwelling outside the Land is better than dwelling in the Land of Israel - for this applies to every person: that he serve his Creator a complete service, a perfect service, and be himself a dwelling place for holiness, as it is written (Exodus 25:8), "and let them make Me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them [betocham]." And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained: it is not said "within it [betocho]" but "among them [betocham]" [i.e., within each person]. And it is written (Jeremiah 7:4): "the temple of the LORD, they are." And they said in the Holy Zohar: happy is the man who makes for the Shechinah a fine dwelling in his heart. And in any case, in his old age, it is a time to be gracious to the soul, to return the deposit to God - whoever has it in his power shall strive to go up to the place of the altar, that there be his death, there be his burial, and let his resting be honorable. For this let him pray all the days of his life, in the manner of the saying of King David, peace be upon him (Psalms 27:4): "one thing I ask of the LORD," and so on, "to behold the pleasantness of the LORD and to visit His Temple" - perhaps the LORD shall hear his voice.
Pele Yoetz 70:1: Worry - It is written (Proverbs 12:25): "worry in a man's heart weighs it down." And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained (Yoma 75a): let him drive it from his mind - or alternatively, let him tell it to others. And both are true: at first let him strive to drive it from his mind with pure thoughts and doubtful claims that exist to dispel the worry, and if he cannot, let him tell it to others, namely Torah scholars and men of knowledge who know how to set him right with good counsel, and who shall speak to him words that dispel the worry and settle the heart - for the sage has already said (Mareh Musar, 5): the past is gone, the future is not yet, from where does worry come? Arise, drink wine [i.e., be at ease]. For if the matter has already passed, what benefit is there in worrying - can he bring it back? Is the evil that has befallen him not enough, that he should add the evil of worry and live a life of hardship? Let him drive it from his mind. And if it is a matter yet to come, if there is a remedy, let him apply the remedy, and if there is no remedy, what benefit is there in worrying? Let him trust in the Name of the LORD and rely on his God. This is a great principle for removing worry.
Pele Yoetz 70:2: And another principle: let him consider and believe with complete faith that no evil thing descends from Heaven, and whatever the Merciful One does, He does for the good (Berachot 60b) - for the good of the soul or the good of the body - and whatever appears to the eyes to be evil, God has considered it for good. Sometimes it is revealed to a person, and he says, "I thank You, for You have answered me and become my salvation" (Psalms 118:21). And sometimes it remains hidden, that the Holy One, blessed be He, wishes to chasten him in order to save him from death and save his soul from going down to the pit. If so, from where does worry come? To what is this comparable? To one who is sentenced to death by the kingdom, and by the king's compassion for him, he agrees to give him a few blows on his legs instead, or to take from him a few coins - certainly he shall accept his sentence with joy and give thanks and praise to the king. So is this matter - for our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Pesachim 118a) on the verse "give thanks to the LORD for He is good," that He collects a person's debt through his own good - his flask breaks, his wine spills, his chicken dies, and the like, a small loss instead of his whole life, and the mercy of God prevails so that even what He takes from him is His own [i.e., a small deduction rather than total loss]. To what is this comparable? To a king who says to his own creditor: all the people know that a debt owed to the king cannot be canceled, but do this instead - take this purse of gold coins and pay your creditors whom you owe me, and you and your children shall live on what remains. Is there a sweeter palate than this? So the Holy One, blessed be He, collects a person's debt through his own good - He gives him and gives him and gives him again, more and more, the Omnipresent fills his lack and the surplus overflowing. The LORD makes poor and makes rich, He wounds and His hand heals, He puts to death and gives life - in a manner that even regarding death there is no need to worry, for the LORD does not put a person to death for his harm but for his good, and His designs are not miscalculated - and if before God, blessed be He, it seems fitting for us, all the more so should we not worry. We have nothing but to say: the LORD, whatever is good in His eyes, for peace of mind before the throne of His glory, He shall do - and it is upon us to accept everything with willingness and joy.
Pele Yoetz 71:1: Words of the Sages - It is known that the words of the Sages are more severe than the words of the Torah, for whoever transgresses the words of the Sages is liable to death (Berachot 4b). And it is because of our sins that many of the common people treat the words of the Sages lightly and transgress them, being wise in their own eyes - such as regarding milk milked by a gentile without a Jew observing, which is forbidden due to concern for impure milk, and the unruly say, what is the reason - is it not because of impure milk? We are witnesses that there is no impure milk here! If only they were wise, they would understand that all the words of the Sages are living and enduring and have no annulment forever, and the Torah was not given for each individual to decide for himself, and in many places they said, the Rabbis did not distinguish [between cases]. And whoever transgresses their words, even if in truth the milk was from a pure animal, some say it is as though he ate carrion and torn animals - and we have nothing but the words of the Sages, for besides the reason according to the plain meaning, there are several hidden secrets within them, and "the integrity of the upright shall guide them" (Proverbs 11:3) - not to deviate from their words, right or left, in prohibitions, enactments, decrees, and good counsels scattered throughout the Talmud, for the spirit of the LORD spoke through them, and whoever listens to them shall dwell securely and tranquilly, undisturbed by fear of evil, and shall find favor and good sense in the eyes of God and man. And I have already, with my own hand and strength, gathered their words scattered throughout the Talmud, the Holy Zohar, the Midrashim, and other books, as the good hand of the LORD was upon me, in the pamphlet "Orot Elim." Happy is the man who listens to me and diligently studies the doors of my aforementioned pamphlet - let the wise man hear and increase learning, and not transgress, for whoever transgresses their words deserves to be liable for his own life, even if he has no sin other than this, that he did not listen to their words and their good counsel. And the mitzvah of listening to their words is fitting to shield him and cause him to succeed in all his ways, Amen.
Pele Yoetz 72:1: Preacher - How good is preaching to the public, but it requires many conditions. This comes out first: that he first pray to be saved from pride and from the evil eye, and that his words bear fruit. And let him also pray that he have an eloquent tongue to speak his words with pleasant conversation, in clear speech, in a manner that his words be pleasant to those who hear them, like a bride who is beloved by her husband, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, wrote (Shir HaShirim Rabbah, ch. 4). And this is second: that he not prolong his trouble, but rather be brief and rise above it - a little of good is enough. And third: that he be careful of people's honor, so that they not come to public shame because of his words, and that he not speak of them erroneously, and not teach an accusation against them - and let him include himself with them, saying, "the way we walk is not good; come, let us walk in the light of the LORD." And let him guard against suspicion, that a listener not suspect him of preaching for his own benefit - and therefore he should not preach excessively about the obligation to give charity to Torah scholars and the honor and reverence due to Torah scholars and the like. And he should always arrange the sermon beforehand by himself, in a manner that it be fluent in his mouth - for sometimes he must skip certain matters that are not fitting to preach in public, or matters he does not understand well at first glance - and if he arranges it, he shall not need to interrupt in the middle, which is a disgrace for a Torah scholar. And let the wise man hear and increase learning - and how good is a word in its proper time.
Pele Yoetz 73:1: Letter Hei: Praise - It is fitting to praise the LORD for all the good He does with us, and even if our mouths were full of song, and so on, we would not suffice to praise Him, and silence itself is His praise. In any case, it is impossible to do nothing at all, and it is fitting for every person, from time to time and from occasion to occasion, to give thanks and praise to the LORD - and especially when recounting some matter he did and succeeded in, let the Name of Heaven immediately be fluent in his mouth, and let him say: praise to God, blessed be He, for He has wondrously shown His kindness to me, and until now He has helped me do such-and-such. Even if he has sufferings, he should praise the LORD that He has made him worthy to be among those whom the LORD loves and rebukes, and that he is not among those to whom He repays their enemies, and that they have not chastened him with harsher and more bitter sufferings - for He is merciful in judgment and collects a person's debt through his own good. And if the LORD has favored him with more good than others, it is fitting for him to praise the LORD, who has favored him with His goodness not through his own merit but through His mercy and compassion, for many better than himself lack all good. And let him humble himself greatly and fix in his heart complete faith that it is He who gives him the strength to do valiantly, and everything is from His hand, and His designs are not miscalculated.
Pele Yoetz 73:2: And all the more so is it fitting for the man whom the LORD has favored with the goods of the soul, and made him worthy to have his portion among those who sit in the study house, and graced him with wisdom and knowledge, to praise the LORD - and above all, if the LORD has graced him to be complete in some good traits and to recognize which is the straight path more than others, whose own way seems straight to them though it leads them astray. And likewise if the LORD has prepared for him some mitzvah and saved him from transgression - these are greater goods than all the life of the World to Come. And if they said (Berachot 34b) regarding a king, that once he bows he does not straighten up again [i.e. maintains a posture of submission], to teach humility before the LORD who has favored him with His goodness - all the more so and how much more so one whom the LORD has favored with goods of the soul, how much more must he humble himself and say, I am unworthy of all the kindnesses, for this too is a gift of God, and he must give thanks to Him and bless in His Name. And this is part of the mitzvah that our Sages, of blessed memory, established for us, to recite Hallel over miracles and deliverance, as the master, author of Sefer "Charedim," wrote. And it is included among the kindnesses of the LORD, and the just ordinances of the LORD that gladden the heart, that we bless Him and praise His Name for the good He does with us - it shall be pleasant to Him, and it shall be counted a mitzvah for us, and we receive reward for it - to the point that they said that whoever has a miracle performed for him and recites a song of praise (see Midrash Tehillim, Shocher Tov, 18:6), behold, his reward is that another miracle is performed for him, as it is said (Psalms 50:23), "a thank-offering," and so on, "I shall show him the salvation of God." Is there a sweeter palate than this? Therefore, "give thanks to the LORD, for He is good, for His kindness endures forever."
Pele Yoetz 73:3: However, regarding praising people, there is in this matter also a "turning away from evil" aspect - such as what is written (Proverbs 28:4), "those who forsake the Torah praise the wicked," which is included in the great evil of flattery, as written in the books and as we have written somewhat in its place. And likewise a man who praises himself falsely - and even one who praises himself truly shall be punished. And in praising the deeds of the righteous there is an aspect of mitzvah, that people hear and learn to do as their deeds, for "the envy of scribes increases wisdom" (Bava Batra 21a). But one must weigh in the balance that a mitzvah not come through a transgression - for example, saying his praise to his face, which could lead to pride and transgress "before the blind"; and likewise if one says his praise in the presence of his enemies, he stumbles into a shade of slander, since through his praise it comes to his disgrace. And likewise one must be careful, when recounting his praise, that it not be in the presence of people who might be feared to cast an evil eye upon him. And likewise one must be careful not to cause loss or any harm to his fellow that would displease him through praising him, in the manner of "one who blesses his fellow with a loud voice, rising early in the morning, it shall be counted a curse to him" (Proverbs 27:14). And sometimes it is fitting to praise him to his face for his good deeds and inform him of the greatness of his mitzvah and its reward, so that he be strengthened in his good custom and continue to add to it - but it is fitting to add in his words, telling him not to credit himself with the good, for this was the purpose of his creation and no person can fully discharge his obligation. And whoever receives a benefit from his fellow should praise and bless him privately and publicly, so as not to be ungrateful - and even for a slice of bread eaten at the host's table, our Rabbis, of blessed memory, established (Berachot 46a) that one should bless the host. And they said (ibid. 55a[?]) that whoever withholds from blessing him shortens his own days and years, as it is written (Genesis 12:3), "and I shall bless those who bless you," as explained in the Talmud - all the more so one who receives from his fellow an extra kindness or any kind of benefit, whether money or money's worth, is obligated to bless him, and through this blessings shall rest upon his own head. And I, the poor one, have already arranged an order of prayer for one who receives a benefit - it is written and I have appended it to my Beit Tefillati, with the help of Heaven. And let him reason a fortiori on that day: all the more so is it fitting to praise and bless the LORD, from whose hand everything comes, and all who benefit him are agents of the Merciful One, and there is no end to His goodness and kindnesses that He does with us every single day continually, and praise befits Him.
Pele Yoetz 74:1: Shaming - It is known how severe is the prohibition of shaming one's fellow's face in public, for one who does so has no share in the World to Come (Bava Metzia 59a). And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 43b): it is better for a person to throw himself into a fiery furnace than to shame his fellow's face in public. And it is because of our sins that many of the common people, when there is a quarrel between men, revile and blaspheme one another, and each one mentions his fellow's faults, what he did wrong in ancient days and past years - and not only that, but he says of him what is not even true in him. And though this is severe from the aspect of spreading a bad name, when he reviles him with what was truly in him it is even more severe - for regarding what is not in him, there is not as much shaming as when he mentions his earlier sins, for "the red departs and the white comes" [i.e., he blushes and pales], and this is like shedding blood. And whoever does this does not return in repentance, since it seems to him that he has no sin, and he says, "what does it matter, I spoke the truth," and does not take to heart that his sin is greater because of the severity of the prohibition of shaming, as stated. And there is one who shames his fellow's face even unknowingly, speaking in his presence in disparagement of faults he has, or in disparagement of deeds he himself did, even though he does not intend this against him - he is caught in the shade of shaming. Therefore silence is fitting, for with much speech, transgression does not cease. However, to keep someone from a prohibition it is permitted - for example, a man who transgresses the words of Torah and is rebuked to his face privately as required, and he persists in his impurity - in the end it is fitting to revile him and blaspheme him and shame him in public, so that he return from his evil way and walk in the way of the good.
Pele Yoetz 75:1: Walking - Walking has in it an aspect of "turning away from evil," in the manner of what is written (Psalms 1:1), "happy is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the wicked," and so on. And as they said (Sotah 22a[?]): when one goes for the sake of a mitzvah, there is reward for the steps, and they said that from every single step an angel is created. This applies correspondingly, conversely, when one goes for the sake of a transgression - and the knowledge of opposites is one. And happy is he who is confined at home, among those who sit in the study house - for walking among people not for the purpose of occupying oneself with Torah is like having one's feet brought into bronze fetters, and the evil inclination has spread a net for his feet, and on his return a heap of creeping things - sins and transgressions - hangs behind him. And behold, the evil inclination teaches many tricks and seventy faces to purify the impure creeping thing, telling him that it is fitting to mix with people for the sake of the ways of peace, and that by going out into public, his eyes shall see and he shall come to know the afflictions of that land and set up fences, and sometimes through such talk some good thing is found, that he speaks words of ethics and fear of the LORD to guide his fellow aright - but the man who fears the LORD should not consent to this, and let his feet lead him to the study house instead, for a certainty is not displaced by a doubt - and let him reckon the loss of the mitzvah he loses by not occupying himself with Torah, for one hour of Torah is precious, and what he loses - that he might come to forbidden speech and forbidden sights and many such evils - outweighs the reward that some mitzvah might perhaps come through his hand. And the man who fears the LORD and greatly desires His mitzvot is credited with merit for being confined at home, since all roads are presumed dangerous, and it is not fitting for a person to go to a place where danger is common even for the sake of a mitzvah (Yoma 11a). And if they said this regarding harm to the body, all the more so regarding harm to the soul.
